subject: Copywriting
title: Consumerism as Ideology
description: A 60-second lesson on Consumerism as Ideology.

hook.text: After WWII, America needed citizens to spend, not save. Advertising became propaganda for a new ideology: consumerism.

buildup.text: Factories that built tanks needed new markets. Advertisers reframed buying as patriotic duty: consume for the economy.

discovery.text: Planned obsolescence was the copywriter's invention.

twist.text: Victor Lebow wrote: 'Our economy demands that we make consumption a way of life.' He said the quiet part out loud.

climax.text: The most successful propaganda isn't political—it's commercial.

punchline.text: Buy for the economy. Consumerism became an ideology sold as freedom.

quiz.question: What did Victor Lebow argue about consumption?
options: Consumption must become a way of life

details.summary: After World War II, advertising transformed from selling products to selling a way of life. Consumerism became an ideology — the belief that happiness, identity, and social status are achieved through purchasing. This was deliberate propaganda designed to fuel economic growth.
details.whyItMatters: Recognizing consumerism as an ideology rather than a natural state of being helps people make more conscious choices about spending, identity, and what truly constitutes a good life.
takeaways: Post-war advertising deliberately promoted consumption as the path to happiness
Planned obsolescence was invented to keep consumers buying
Consumerism serves economic systems more than individual well-being

faq.question: How did consumerism become an ideology?
faq.answer: After WWII, industrial capacity needed new outlets. Advertising agencies, economists, and governments collaborated to promote the idea that buying things was patriotic, personally fulfilling, and the measure of success. What was once a marketing strategy became a cultural belief system.

faq.question: Who benefits from consumerism as ideology?
faq.answer: Corporations benefit from constant demand, governments benefit from economic growth and tax revenue, and media benefits from advertising spending. Consumers receive temporary satisfaction but often find that purchases don't deliver the lasting happiness promised.
